[[Image:A_Blind_Beggar_(1878)_-_TIMEA.jpg|thumb|right|Blind Egyptian beggar|upright=1.2]]

From {{inh|cop|egx-dem|bnjt||date palm}}
[[File:Date palm leaf.jpg|thumb|right|Date palm leaf]]

[[Image:Ancient_Egypt_Medical_tools4.jpg|thumb|right|Egyptian surgical saws]]

Apparently from a descendant of {{der|cop|sem-pro|*paḥal-}}, whose {{cog|ar|-}} descendant {{m|ar|فَحْل}} beside a male camel and virile man also means a male palm-tree, and a modification of which {{m|ar|بَلَح}} is used for fresh dates; direct borrowings are phonologically and chronologically difficult.

definitions: * {{Q|cop|||Matthew 6:12|quote=ⲛⲅ̄ⲕⲱ ⲛⲁⲛ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧ'''ⲉⲣⲟⲛ''' ⲛ̄ⲑⲉ ϩⲱⲱⲛ ⲟⲛ ⲉⲧⲉⲛⲕⲱ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲉⲟⲩⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲛ '''ⲉⲣⲟⲟⲩ'''.|t=And forgive us our debts (literally ''"those (things) which are '''due from us'''"''), as we also have forgiven our debtors (literally ''"those '''from whom''' we have (something) '''due'''"'').}}

Usage notes.content: ⲉ- is used instead of the direct object particle {{m|cop|ⲛ-|ⲛ̄-}} in some functionally transitive verbs. This is common in verbs of perception.

Etymology.etymology_text:
<div>From {{inh|cop|egx-dem||{{t2i-Egyd|ꜣ|b|y|n-2|A14}}|tr={{l|egx-dem|ꜣbyn}}|poor man}}. Ultimately borrowed from {{bor|cop|sem-can|}} ''*ʾabyōn-'',<ref>{{cite-journal|last=Wilson-Wright|first=Aren M.|last2=Huehnergard|first2=John|title=How to Kill a Dragon in Northwest Semitic: Three Linguistic Observations regarding Ugaritic ltn and Hebrew liwyātān|journal=Vetus Testamentum|volume=72|issue=1|year=2021|doi=10.1163/15685330-bja10047|titleurl=https://brill.com/view/journals/vt/72/1/article-p151_8.xml|publisher=Brill|passage=Normally, the suffix ''*-ān'' becomes ''-ôn'' in Biblical Hebrew with the operation of the Canaanite shift (e.g., ''*ʔabyān-'' > ''ʔebyôn'' “poor”).}}</ref>
 whence also {{der|cop|he|אֶבְיוֹן|tr=ʾeḇyōn|t=poor, needy}}. Related to {{cog|uga|𐎀𐎁𐎊𐎐|t=poor, impoverished|ts=ʾabyānu}}.<ref>{{cite-book|last=Bordreuil|first=Pierre|last2=Pardee|first2=Dennis|title=A Manual of Ugaritic|page=293|text=ʾABYN adjective 'destitute, poor' /ʾabyānu/|publisher=Penn State Press|isbn= 1575066521|year=2009}}</ref><div>
A {{bor|cop|sem}} borrowing, ultimately from {{der|cop|sem-pro|*baraḳ-}}. Compare {{cog|he|בָּרָק|tr=bārā́q}}, {{cog|arc|בַּרְקָא}}, and {{cog|ar|بَرْق}}.
A {{bor|cop|sem}} borrowing, ultimately from {{der|cop|sem-pro|*baraḳ-}}. Compare {{cog|he|בָּרָק|tr=bārā́q}}, {{cog|arc|בַּרְקָא}}, and {{cog|ar|بَرْق}}.

Usage notes.content: ⲉⲑⲱϣ denominates "black person", living in the parts of Africa south of the Aswan, i.e. the Horn of Africa and Sudan. In the Septuagint, {{l|cop|ⲡⲕⲁϩⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲛⲓⲉ̀ⲑⲁⲩϣ|t=land of the Ethiopians}} and {{l|cop|ⲛⲓⲉⲑⲁⲩϣ}} translates {{cog|hbo|כּוּשׁ}} (kûš) and {{cog|grc|Αἰθιοπία}}, the Biblical term for "black Africa". In the latter Coptic literature and toponymy ⲉⲑⲱϣ is used as an equivalent of {{cog|ar|حبش|tr=habaš|t=Abyssinian}}.

==Coptic== ===Alternative forms=== * {{alter|cop|ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲣⲁⲛ||to a female, Bohairic}} * {{alter|cop|ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲁⲛ||to a female, Sahidic}} ===Etymology===
From {{inh|cop|egy||n:y-G20-A2-r:N35-A2-k|tr={{m|egy|njm}} {{m|egy|rn}}{{m|egy|.k}}}}, with replacement of the possessive suffix .k “you” by the possessive adjective {{inh|cop|egy||G40-i-i-k|tr={{m|egy|pꜣy}}{{m|egy|.k}}}} and the addition of the copula ⲡⲉ derived from {{inh|cop|egy||G40-i-i|tr={{m|egy|pꜣy}}}}.
===Phrase=== {{head|cop|phrase}} # [[what is your name]]? #* Genesis 32:27 (Bohairic) #*: ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ ⲇⲉ ⲛⲁϥ ϫⲉ '''ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲁⲛ''' #*:: "But he said to him, 'What is your name?'" #* Luke 8:30 (Sahidic) #*: ⲁ ⲓⲥ ϫⲛⲟⲩϥ ϫⲉ '''ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲁⲛ''' #*:: "Jesus asked him, 'What is your name?'" ====Usage notes==== ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲁⲛ (lit.ː Who your name) and its feminine variants are the standard way to express "What is your name", "What are you called" in Coptic. Under the influence of modern languages like English, *ⲁϣ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲁⲛ (lit.: "What is your name") has become common in revivalist circles. This is, however, not the regular expression in Coptic materials from the time when Coptic was still actively written by native speakers.

#* Luke 8:30 (Sahidic)
#*: ⲁ ⲓⲥ ϫⲛⲟⲩϥ ϫⲉ '''ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲁⲛ'''
#*:: "Jesus asked him, 'What is your name?'"

Usage notes.content: ⲛⲓⲙ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲁⲛ (lit.ː Who your name) and its feminine variants are the standard way to express "What is your name", "What are you called" in Coptic. Under the influence of modern languages like English, *ⲁϣ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲁⲛ (lit.: "What is your name") has become common in revivalist circles. This is, however, not the regular expression in Coptic materials from the time when Coptic was still actively written by native speakers.

References.content: * TLA lemma no. C2479 (ⲛⲟⲙⲧⲉ), in: Coptic Dictionary Online, ed. by the Koptische/Coptic Electronic Language and Literature International Alliance (KELLIA), https://coptic-dictionary.org/entry.cgi?tla=C2479 (accessed 2024-09-16).

Etymology.etymology_text: From {{inh|cop|egx-dem|s-ḥmt||woman}}, from {{inh|cop|egy|zt-ḥmt||woman}}, from {{m|egy|zt|z:t*B1|tr={{m|egy|zt}}|woman}} + {{m|egy|ḥmt|N41:t-B1|tr={{m|egy|ḥmt}}|wife, woman}}, a compound that arose because the feminine ending {{m|egy|-t}} in {{m|egy|zt}} eventually became silent, making {{m|egy|zt}} homophonous with {{m|egy|z||man}}, so that it became necessary to add {{m|egy|ḥmt}} to distinguish between them. {{surf|cop|ⲥⲁ|ϩⲓⲙⲉ}}.

From {{inh|cop|egx-dem|s-ḥmt||woman}}, from {{inh|cop|egy|zt-ḥmt||woman}}, from {{m|egy|zt|z:t*B1|tr={{m|egy|zt}}|woman}} + {{m|egy|ḥmt|N41:t-B1|tr={{m|egy|ḥmt}}|wife, woman}}, a compound that arose because the feminine ending {{m|egy|-t}} in {{m|egy|zt}} eventually became silent, making {{m|egy|zt}} homophonous with {{m|egy|z||man}}, so that it became necessary to add {{m|egy|ḥmt}} to clarify.
From {{inh|cop|egx-dem|sḏy||to speak, to tell}}, from {{inh|cop|egy|sḏd||to recount}} s-D&d-A2, related to {{m|egy|ḏd|gloss=to speak, say}}.

Etymology.etymology_text: A hypothetical correction of the attested {{l|cop|ϯⲕⲉϣⲣⲱⲙⲓ}} which is {{compound|cop|ϯ|ⲕⲱϣ|ⲣⲱⲙⲓ||pos1= feminine definite article|pos2=verb|pos3=noun|gloss2=break|gloss3=man}}, lit. "the men breaker". {{calque|cop|ar|القَاهِرَة|t=The Victorious}}.

Derived either  from {{compound|cop|ϯ|ⲕⲱϣ|ⲣⲱⲙⲓ||pos1= feminine definite article|pos2=verb|pos3=noun|gloss2=break|gloss3=man}}, lit. definitions: *:: "Do you believe, '''King Agrippa''', in the prophets? I know that you do believe."
*: "Ⲉⲓϩⲓ ⲡⲓⲙⲱⲓⲧ ⲇⲉ ϧⲉⲛ ̀ⲧⲫⲁϣⲓ ̀ⲙⲡⲓ̀ⲉϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲁⲓⲛⲁⲩ, '''̀ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ''', ̀ⲉⲟⲩⲟⲩⲱⲓⲛⲓ ̀ⲉⲃⲟⲗϧⲉⲛ ̀ⲧⲫⲉ ̀ⲉϩⲟⲧⲉ ̀ⲫⲣⲏ ⲁϥ̀ⲓ ̀ⲉ̀ϩⲣⲏⲓ ̀ⲉϫⲱⲓ ⲛⲉⲙ ⲛⲏⲉⲑⲛⲉⲙⲏⲓ".
*:: "On the road at midday I saw, '''O King''', a light from heaven, brighter than the brightness of the sun, shining round about me and those who journeyed with me.".
*: Ⲟⲩⲟϩ ⲡⲉϫⲉ ⲫⲏⲥⲧⲟⲥ ϫⲉ "'''̀ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲁⲅⲣⲓⲡⲡⲁ''' ⲛⲉⲙ ⲛⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ ⲧⲏⲣⲟⲩ ⲉⲑⲛⲉⲙⲁⲛ ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲛⲁⲩ ̀ⲉⲫⲁⲓ ⲉⲑⲃⲏⲧϥ ̀ⲁ ⲡⲓⲙⲏϣ ⲧⲏⲣϥ ̀ⲛⲧⲉ ⲛⲓⲒⲟⲩⲇⲁⲓ ̀ⲥ̀ⲉⲙⲓ ⲛⲏⲓ ϧⲉⲛ Ⲓⲉⲣⲟⲩⲥⲁⲗⲏⲙ ⲛⲉⲙ ϧⲉⲛ ⲡⲁⲓⲕⲉⲙⲁ ⲉⲩⲱϣ ̀ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϫⲉ ̀ϥⲉⲙ̀ⲡϣⲁ ̀ⲛⲱⲛϧ ⲁⲛ ϫⲉ."

*:: And Festus said, "'''King Agrippa''' and all men who are here present with us, you see this man about whom all the multitude of the Jews have applied to me, both at Jerusalem and also here, crying out that he ought not to live any longer."
*: ̀Ⲉⲧⲁϥⲥⲱⲧⲉⲙ ϫⲉ ̀ⲛϫⲉ ''' ̀ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ Ⲏⲣⲱⲇⲏⲥ''', ⲁϥ̀ϣⲑⲟⲣⲧⲉⲣ, ⲛⲉⲙ Ⲓⲉⲣⲟⲩⲥⲁⲗⲏⲙ ⲧⲏⲣⲥ ⲛⲉⲙⲁϥ.
*:: When '''King Herod''' heard this, he was troubled, and all of Jerusalem with him.
*: Ⲉϥⲉⲣⲁⲡⲟⲗⲟⲅⲓⲥⲑⲉ ̀ⲛϫⲉ ⲡⲁⲩⲗⲟⲥ ϫⲉ "ⲟⲩⲇⲉ ̀ⲙⲟⲩⲉⲣⲛⲟⲃⲓ ̀ⲉ̀ⲫⲛⲟⲙⲟⲥ ̀ⲛⲛⲓⲒⲟⲩⲇⲁⲓ, ⲟⲩⲇⲉ ⲡⲓⲉⲣⲫⲉⲓ, ⲟⲩⲇⲉ''' ̀ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ'''".
*:: While Paul answered for himself: "Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor yet against '''Caesar'''."
* The Martyrdom of John of Phanijoit
*: ...ϧⲉⲛ ⲡ̀ⲉ̀ϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲙ̀ⲡⲉ̅ ϧⲉⲛ ϯⲁϫⲡⲋ̅ ⲧⲉ ⲛⲁϩⲣⲁϥ '''ⲙ̀ⲡⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲉⲗⲭⲉⲙⲏⲗ''' ⲡϣⲏⲣⲓ '''ⲙ̀ⲡ̀ⲟⲩⲣⲟ ⲉⲗⲁⲧⲉⲗ''' ⲡⲓⲡⲉⲣⲥⲏⲥ ⲁⲣⲁⲃⲟⲥ ϧⲉⲛ ⲡ̀ⲑ̀ⲣⲟⲛⲟⲥ ⲙ̀ⲡⲓⲃⲁⲛ...

Usage notes.content:
* Used to mark long vowels: ''ā'' = [aː], ''ē'' = [ɛː] or [æː], ''ī'' = [iː], ''ū'' = [uː].
* For a short while (1908–1919), it was also used with the letter ''o'' (''ō'') to mark long [oː] in words of foreign origin, but this usage has since then been abandoned.
* Letters with macrons are considered as separate letters with different names, and listed in the alphabet after the same letters without macron (i.e., ''ā'' after ''a'', ''ē'' after ''e'', ''ī'' after ''i'', and ''ū'' after ''u''). In actual practice, however, letters with and without macrons are treated as the same letter in alphabetized lists (e.g., in dictionaries), unlike letters with cedillas (''ģ'', ''ķ'', ''ļ'', ''ņ'') or háčeks (''č'', ''š'', ''ž''), which are kept separate in alphabetized lists.
